title: The Universe and the Stars
description: Ten standalone texts about the night sky: a dark-sky park, the life of stars, an amateur astronomer, the telescope, black holes, distant planets, the northern lights, comets, life in orbit and a famous moonlit trial.

lessons.title: A Night at the Dark-Sky Park
lessons.summary: A grandmother takes her thirteen-year-old grandson to a dark-sky park in the desert, where a ranger shows them the Milky Way.
lessons.text:
Last October, I took my grandson, Leo, on a trip he had been asking about for months. Leo had just turned thirteen, and in his opinion, thirteen was old enough to see a truly dark sky. So we drove five hours into the desert, to a dark-sky park: a place protected from artificial light, so that the stars can be seen the way people saw them centuries ago.

Leo rode shotgun the whole way. In our family, riding shotgun simply means sitting in the front passenger seat, and my grandson took the job seriously: he held the map and chose the music.

The sign outside our motel said "No Vacancy," but I had booked our room weeks earlier. The owner told us that on clear weekends there is rarely a vacancy anywhere near the park, because so many people now travel to see the stars.

Before sunset, we walked along a trail between tall fins of red rock. A fin, a ranger told us, is a narrow wall of stone shaped by wind and water over millions of years. A sign at the start of the trail asked visitors to stay on the path, because the land had once been a military range. An old grenade might still lie under the sand, and anyone who saw a grenade was asked not to touch it but to report it to a ranger. Leo stayed in the very middle of the path after that.

Far beyond the park, a line of wind turbines stood on a ridge. Each turbine had a small red light on top, blinking slowly to warn aircraft.

When night fell, about forty people gathered in an open field. The ranger held a green laser pointer, and its thin beam seemed to reach all the way to the stars. With the pointer, she traced the shape of the Summer Triangle and then moved it slowly along the Milky Way, our own galaxy seen from the inside.

I had seen photographs of the Milky Way, but nothing had prepared me for the real thing. It stretched from one side of the sky to the other, like a river of light. Leo lay on his back and gazed up without a word. I lay next to him and gazed too. For a while, I felt overwhelmed, the way people feel at the edge of the ocean: small, but not in a sad way. Leo was overwhelmed too, by the sheer number of stars, which seemed to grow every time he looked.

Near midnight, we walked back to the car. Leo asked whether we could come back next year, and I promised that he could ride shotgun again.

Questions:
How old was Leo, and why did he want to see a dark sky?
He was thirteen, and he believed that thirteen was old enough to see a truly dark sky.
What does riding shotgun mean in the writer's family?
It means sitting in the front passenger seat.
Why were visitors asked to stay on the path?
The land had once been part of a military range, and an old grenade might still lie under the sand.
What did the ranger do with the green laser pointer?
She traced the Summer Triangle and moved it along the Milky Way.
How did the writer feel when she saw the Milky Way?
She felt overwhelmed, small but not sad, as people feel at the edge of the ocean.

lessons.title: How a Star Is Born and How It Dies
lessons.summary: An explanation of how clouds of gas spawn new stars, how stars live, and how their mass decides the way they die.
lessons.text:
Every star in the night sky began its life inside a cloud. These clouds are made mostly of hydrogen gas, with a little dust mixed in. They are cold and enormous, often many light-years across, and a single cloud can spawn hundreds or even thousands of stars.

Something, perhaps the shock wave from a star exploding nearby, pushes parts of the cloud together, and denser lumps begin to form. Once a lump holds enough matter, its own gravity takes over. Gravity pulls the gas toward the center, and as the lump shrinks, gravity tightens its grip even more. When the center reaches about 10 million degrees, hydrogen atoms start to fuse, releasing huge amounts of energy. At that moment, a star is born.

For a long time, a young star stays embedded in the cloud that made it, hidden behind a thick curtain of dust. Ordinary telescopes cannot see these embedded stars, but infrared telescopes can look through the dust.

Then comes maturity. A star spends about 90 percent of its life in this stage, quietly fusing hydrogen in its core. Our Sun reached maturity long ago and has been shining for about 4.6 billion years.

To understand how a star dies, astronomers differentiate between stars by their mass, because mass decides almost everything. If we arranged all the stars of our galaxy by mass, they would form a pyramid. At the narrow top of the pyramid sit a few giant stars, many times heavier than the Sun. Stars like the Sun fill the middle. The broad base of the pyramid is made of small, cool red dwarfs, which make up about three quarters of all stars.

Red dwarfs are undoubtedly the hardy survivors of the universe. They burn their fuel so slowly that they can shine for trillions of years. Not one of these hardy stars has ever died, because the universe, at 13.8 billion years old, is simply too young.

A star like the Sun has a gentler end. In about 5 billion years, the Sun will swell into a red giant and throw off a large chunk of its outer layers into space. What remains will be a white dwarf, a hot core about the size of Earth that slowly cools.

The giants at the top of the pyramid have the most violent end. When their fuel runs out, their cores collapse in less than a second, and the star explodes. The explosion spreads chunks of new elements, such as iron and oxygen, across space. In time, these elements may join a new cloud and spawn new stars and planets. The story of a star, then, can encompass billions of years, and it may encompass us too: the iron in your blood was undoubtedly made inside stars long before the Earth existed. Mass, in the end, is what lets us differentiate a quiet death from a violent one.

Questions:
What are the clouds that spawn stars made of?
They are made mostly of hydrogen gas, with a little dust.
What happens when a lump in a cloud holds enough matter?
Its gravity pulls the gas toward the center and tightens its grip, until the center is hot enough for atoms to fuse.
Why can't ordinary telescopes see very young stars?
The young stars are embedded in the cloud, behind a thick curtain of dust.
What would the stars look like if they were arranged by mass?
They would form a pyramid, with a few giants at the top and many red dwarfs at the base.

lessons.title: The Footballer Who Watches the Sky
lessons.summary: A profile of a former soccer player from England who became a carpenter in Oregon and now measures stars for science from his backyard.
lessons.text:
Graham Webb spent his first career looking at the ground in front of him, and his second career looking up. For twelve years he was a professional footballer in England. In the United States, he would be called a soccer player. He was fast, rarely scored and never stopped running. Today he lives on a quiet road in Oregon, and on clear nights he can usually be found in a small wooden observatory behind his house.

Graham grew up in a coal town in the Midlands, the region in the middle of England. "In the Midlands, the sky was always orange from the street lights," he says. "I didn't know there were so many stars until I was twenty."

When his knees ended his life as a footballer, Graham moved to the United States with his wife, who was born in Oregon, and trained as a carpenter. The work suited him. "A carpenter and a footballer need the same thing: you do the same simple movement a thousand times until it's right."

The observatory is his own work. He built it from maple, cut from trees that a storm had knocked down on his land, and the maple walls still smell sweet. Above the door hangs a sign that he carved himself, with the words "Clear Skies" carved deep into the wood. In the evenings, his wife sits on the back porch with a cup of tea while Graham works, and the light from the porch is the only one he allows near the observatory.

What does an amateur do with a telescope? Graham measures variable stars, stars whose light grows brighter and fainter over days or years. Every clear night, he records how bright certain stars are and sends the numbers to an international database that professional researchers use.

He believes the right mindset matters more than the equipment. "It's the footballer's mindset," he says. "You turn up, you do the work, you don't complain about the weather." When people tell him that amateurs cannot do real science anymore, he smiles. "Rubbish," he says, in the accent of the Midlands. "Absolute rubbish. Much of what we know about variable stars comes from people in their backyards."

Members of the local astronomy club envy his dark skies, but they envy his patience even more. To them he has become a kind of guru, the person to call when a telescope will not focus or a measurement looks wrong. Graham laughs at the word guru. "I'm a carpenter who stays up late," he says.

What pleases him most is teaching. Twice a month, children from the local school visit the observatory. He wants to motivate them the way a good coach would, by letting them try things themselves. Nothing, he believes, can motivate a child like a first look at the rings of Saturn.

Questions:
What was Graham's first career?
He was a professional footballer in England for twelve years.
Why did Graham not see many stars as a boy?
In the Midlands, the sky was always orange from the street lights.
What is Graham's observatory made of?
It is made of maple from trees that a storm had knocked down on his land.
What does Graham do with his telescope?
He measures variable stars and sends the numbers to a database that researchers use.
Why do club members see Graham as a guru?
He is the person they call when a telescope will not focus or a measurement looks wrong.

lessons.title: A Short History of the Telescope
lessons.summary: How the telescope grew from a Dutch invention into the great instruments that showed mankind the size of the universe.
lessons.text:
In 1608, a Dutch lens maker asked the government for a patent on a new device: a tube with two lenses that made distant objects look closer. Word of the invention spread quickly across Europe. Within a year, it reached a professor in Italy named Galileo Galilei.

Galileo built his own telescope, and then better ones, until his instruments made objects look about twenty times closer. In the autumn of 1609, he did something few people had thought of: he pointed his telescope at the night sky. With that simple act, he embarked on one of the most important journeys in the history of science, and mankind embarked on it with him.

What he saw changed everything. The Moon had mountains and valleys. Four small moons circled the planet Jupiter, which proved that not everything in the sky moved around the Earth. Some scholars thought it foolish to trust a tube of glass over the wisdom of the ancients, and at least one refused to look through it at all, which seems far more foolish to us today.

Galileo's discoveries were part of a quiet revolt against the old view that the Earth stood still at the center of the universe. He noticed that the planet Venus showed phases, like the Moon. The phases corresponded exactly to what a Sun-centered model predicted, and the observation became one of the first nails in the coffin of the Earth-centered model, although it took decades to close that coffin, and the revolt had a price. Galileo saw the phases of Venus as strong justification for his ideas, but the Church demanded more justification than he could give, and in 1633 he was put on trial and spent his last years under house arrest. He had to navigate a dangerous world of politics and religion, and he did not always navigate it well.

Galileo corresponded with scholars across Europe, including the German astronomer Johannes Kepler, who wrote a long letter supporting his discoveries.

Early telescopes used lenses, which bent light but also spread it into colors. In 1668, Isaac Newton built a telescope with a curved mirror instead. Mirrors could be made much larger than lenses, and size mattered, because to see faint objects, astronomers had to maximize the amount of light they collected. The history of the telescope ever since has been a race to maximize the size of the mirror.

Such mirrors were expensive. In the United States around 1900, millionaires paid for some of the greatest instruments. One millionaire, a businessman from Los Angeles named John Hooker, funded a telescope with a mirror 100 inches wide. In 1924, using that telescope, Edwin Hubble showed that some faint clouds of light were whole galaxies far beyond our own. Once again, the telescope had shown mankind a universe far larger than anyone had imagined.

Questions:
What did Galileo do in the autumn of 1609?
He pointed his telescope at the night sky and embarked on a journey of discovery.
What did Galileo see around Jupiter?
He saw four small moons circling the planet.
Why were the phases of Venus important?
They corresponded to a model with the Sun at the center, so they became a nail in the coffin of the Earth-centered model.
Why did Newton use a mirror instead of a lens?
Mirrors could be made much larger, which helped astronomers maximize the light they collected.
Who paid for some of the greatest telescopes in the United States?
Millionaires, such as John Hooker, paid for them.

lessons.title: What Is a Black Hole?
lessons.summary: An explanation of what a black hole is, how big it is, and what it does and does not do to the things around it.
lessons.text:
A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing can escape from it. Light is the fastest thing in the universe, yet even light is not excluded from this rule. That is why a black hole is black.

Most black holes form when a very massive star dies. Its core collapses under its own weight, and an immense amount of matter is squeezed into a tiny space. The result is an object with an immense pull but almost no size.

The edge of a black hole is called the event horizon. It is not a surface you could stand on, but a boundary: outside it, escape is still possible; inside it, nothing is excluded from the fall. The size of the horizon is described by its radius, and the radius depends only on the black hole's mass. For a black hole with the mass of our Sun, the radius would be about 3 kilometers. If the whole Earth could be squeezed into a black hole, its radius would be less than a centimeter, smaller than a marble.

Far from a black hole, its gravity behaves like that of any other object. Close to it, however, gravity rises sharply. The difference in pull between your head and your feet would grow so sharply that you would be stretched out like a piece of soft candy. A star that wanders too close is liable to be torn apart, and astronomers have watched this happen in distant galaxies, where a sudden flash of light can last for months.

Once something crosses the horizon, struggling is pointless. Firing a rocket would be pointless too, because inside the horizon, every possible path leads toward the center.

A common picture shows a black hole as a cosmic vacuum cleaner that will scoop up everything around it. This picture is wrong. A black hole does not reach out to scoop up stars from far away. If the Sun were somehow replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth would keep moving in exactly the same orbit. It would become very cold and dark, but it would not fall in.

Black holes are not rare. There is one in the midst of our own galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth, with a mass about four million times that of the Sun. Almost every large galaxy seems to have one in its midst. In 2022, scientists published the first image of it: a dark shadow surrounded by a ring of glowing gas.

Many questions remain. Physicists still do not know what happens at the very center, where our theories stop working. Some have suggested that, at the tiniest scales, space itself might bubble like foam, appearing and disappearing in ways we cannot see. No one has yet tested this idea of space as foam, but it shows how much is still unknown about these immense, silent objects.

Questions:
Why is a black hole black?
Nothing can escape from it, and even light is not excluded.
What does the radius of a black hole depend on?
It depends only on the black hole's mass.
What is a star that wanders too close liable to do?
It is liable to be torn apart.
Will a black hole scoop up everything around it?
No, it does not reach out to scoop up stars from far away.
What lies in the midst of our galaxy?
A black hole with a mass about four million times that of the Sun lies there.

lessons.title: Searching for Other Worlds
lessons.summary: A science writer remembers when no planets were known around other stars and explains how astronomers now find them.
lessons.text:
When I was fourteen, I owned a poster of the solar system, and I believed that it showed every planet anyone would ever know. No one had yet found a planet around a star like our Sun. Today, more than 6,000 have been found.

The first planet around a Sun-like star was announced in 1995. It was not seen directly; planets are far too faint, and their proximity to their bright stars makes them almost impossible to see. Instead, astronomers noticed that the star itself was moving. As a planet circles a star, its gravity pulls the star in a small circle too. When the star moves toward us, its light shifts slightly toward blue. During its recession, when it moves away from us, the light shifts toward red. Astronomers measured this pattern of approach and recession and worked out the planet's mass and orbit.

That planet was strange. It was a giant, like Jupiter, but it circled its star in just four days. If anyone lived there, a yearly holiday would come around every four days, and a person would celebrate a birthday more than 80 times in a single Earth year. Its yearly journey was short because of its proximity to its star, which made it hotter than any oven.

A second method watches for shadows. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims very slightly, often by less than 1 percent. The line the planet follows across the face of the star is called a chord, the same word that describes a straight line across a circle. A long chord across the middle of the star produces a long dip in its light; a short chord near the edge produces a short one.

A single dip proves nothing, since a fault in the camera can cause one too. Critically, the dips must repeat. If they come at exactly the same intervals, again and again, and if they coincide with small movements of the star itself, astronomers can be confident they have found a planet. When the results of two methods coincide, doubt falls away.

These methods are selective. They find large planets close to their stars much more easily than small planets far away, so the planets we know are a selective sample of what is out there.

The search is now focused on planets like the Earth: rocky worlds at just the right distance from their stars for water to stay liquid. One of them circles Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun. Its proximity, about four light-years away, makes it a critically important target. For someone who once believed in a poster of nine planets, the question of what we will find there is itself a gift.

Questions:
What did the writer believe at fourteen?
The writer believed that the poster showed every planet anyone would ever know.
How did astronomers find the first planet around a Sun-like star?
They measured the star's movement, the pattern of approach and recession in its light.
Why would a yearly holiday come every four days on that planet?
The planet circled its star in just four days because of its proximity to the star.
What is a chord in the second method?
It is the line the planet follows across the face of the star.
Why are these methods called selective?
They find large planets close to their stars much more easily than small planets far away.

lessons.title: The Merry Dancers
lessons.summary: A visitor spends Christmas in the far north of Scotland, where an old fisherman shows her the northern lights and explains what causes them.
lessons.text:
I spent last Christmas in a small village in the far north of Scotland, in a stone house that belonged to an old fisherman named Alasdair and his wife, Morag. I had come for one reason: to see the northern lights. Alasdair promised me that if the sky stayed clear, I would see them.

Morag had hung holly over the door and above the fire, and the dark green holly leaves with their red berries brightened the small kitchen. When I arrived, she greeted me with "Merry Christmas," a week early, as if the holiday had already begun.

On my third night, Alasdair knocked on my door just after ten. "They're out," he said. Outside, the glass of my car was white with frost, and I had to scrape it before we could drive to the cliffs. I was still scraping when the first green light appeared over the sea.

We parked on a hill covered in heather. In summer, Alasdair told me, the heather turns the hills purple, but in December it was brown and stiff with frost. At first, the light was only a pale green band low over the water. Then it grew. A long green slash cut across the sky from east to west, and soon a second slash appeared above it. The bands began to move, slowly at first, then faster, until the whole display became lively, folding and unfolding like a curtain in the wind.

"In these parts," Alasdair said, "people call them the merry dancers." I understood why. They were as lively as dancers at a wedding.

Alasdair also knew the science, which he had read about during long winters on shore. "Every fisherman up here learns a bit of it," he said. The Sun, he explained, throws off a constant stream of tiny particles, some with a negative charge and some positively charged. When this stream, the solar wind, reaches the Earth, our planet's magnetic field guides many of the particles toward the north and south poles. There they crash into gas high in the air, about 100 kilometers up or more. The gas glows: oxygen gives the common green light and, higher up, a deep red; nitrogen adds touches of blue and purple. "So it's the Sun, really," he said, "positively throwing light at us from 150 million kilometers away."

As we watched, the old fisherman told me about the night, forty years earlier, when the lights had been so bright that he could see the fishing line on his reel. He had stopped turning the reel and simply looked up, and his boat had drifted for an hour while he watched.

When we drove home, my head was reeling with colors. Morag had made hot chocolate, and we sat by the fire under the holly. It was the merriest Christmas I can remember.

Questions:
Why did the writer go to the north of Scotland?
She went to see the northern lights.
What did the hills of heather look like in December?
The heather was brown and stiff with frost.
What do people in that part of Scotland call the northern lights?
They call them the merry dancers.
What causes the green light, according to Alasdair?
Particles from the Sun crash into oxygen high in the air, and the oxygen glows green.
What did Alasdair see on his reel forty years earlier?
He could see the fishing line on his reel because the lights were so bright.

lessons.title: What Comets Meant
lessons.summary: What comets really are, and how people in ancient Rome and in 1910 read meaning into them.
lessons.text:
A comet is a lump of ice and dust, usually a few kilometers across, that travels around the Sun on a long, stretched orbit. When its path brings it close to the Sun, the ice begins to turn into gas. The comet starts to expel gas and dust into space, and sunlight pushes this material away, forming a tail that can stretch for millions of kilometers. The closer a comet comes to the Sun, the more material it expels and the brighter it shines.

Comets appear without warning and change from night to night, so for thousands of years people saw them as signs, messages from the gods. One of the most famous appeared in Rome in 44 BC. A few months earlier, Julius Caesar had been killed by a group of senators. His assassination shocked the city. Some Romans saw his killers as heroes who had saved the republic; others saw them as traitors who had murdered a great leader.

In July of that year, Caesar's young heir, Octavian, held public games in Caesar's honor. During the games, a bright comet appeared in the sky and stayed for several nights. Octavian quickly announced that it was the soul of Caesar rising to join the gods. His partisans spread the story across Rome, and coins were made showing a star. In this version, Caesar was a heroic figure who now lived among the gods, and those who had planned the assassination were nothing but traitors. In the hands of Octavian's partisans, the comet became a powerful political tool.

Historians see the episode as a clever piece of political manipulation. Octavian did not make the comet appear, of course, but he gave it a meaning that served him. Many years later, as the emperor Augustus, he was still remembered as the son of a god. The manipulation worked because people wanted to believe that the sky cared about human events. It is an old and comforting idea, a kind of cosmic karma, in which the heavens reward heroic deeds and punish crimes. The idea of karma in the stars is attractive, but comets follow their orbits whatever happens on Earth.

Fear of comets lasted much longer than ancient Rome. In 1910, the Earth was expected to pass through the tail of Halley's Comet. Scientists had found a poison gas in comet tails, and some newspapers suggested that the gas might kill everyone on the planet. Clever sellers offered "comet pills" to protect buyers. Astronomers explained that the tail was so thin that it could do no harm, and they were right. The Earth passed through it without anyone noticing.

Today, we know why comets shine. Yet when a bright comet hangs in the evening sky, it is easy to understand why people once searched it for a message.

Questions:
What happens to a comet when it comes close to the Sun?
Its ice turns into gas, and it starts to expel gas and dust, forming a tail.
What event shocked Rome in 44 BC?
The assassination of Julius Caesar shocked the city.
What did Octavian say the comet was?
He said it was the soul of Caesar rising to join the gods.
Why do historians call the episode a piece of manipulation?
Octavian gave the comet a meaning that served his own political goals.
What did some people buy in 1910?
They bought "comet pills" to protect themselves from gas in the comet's tail.

lessons.title: Six Months Above the Earth
lessons.summary: An astronaut's diary entries from the International Space Station, about exercise, food, history and missing her family.
lessons.text:
Day 1. We reached the International Space Station this afternoon, after a journey of about a day. My daughter, Sofia, gave me a small teddy bear before I left, and I tied it to my seat. When the engines stopped and the teddy began to float in front of me, we knew we had reached orbit. Crews often carry a small toy for exactly this reason.

Day 9. My body is still learning to live without weight. Without gravity pulling fluids down, blood and water move up toward the head, and my face looks puffy in the mirror. The heart also has less work to do, so the cardiovascular system becomes weaker over time. To protect our hearts and bones, we exercise for about two hours every day. I run on a treadmill with straps over my shoulders that hold me down, and I ride a bicycle that has no seat.

Day 23. Everything here has a procedure, and every procedure is written down. The station's handbook is not a single book but thousands of pages on a computer, and I check the handbook before I open a panel or change a filter.

Day 37. Tonight we had tacos. Bread is rarely eaten on the station, because crumbs float away and can get into equipment. Tortillas do not make crumbs, so we use them for almost everything. Tacos have become our Friday tradition. We filled them with beans and chicken, and we laughed as we chased a bean across the room.

Day 58. Today was my first spacewalk. It was the most stressful day of my life, and also the most beautiful. For seven hours, I worked outside the station on a broken unit while the Earth turned below me. Every movement had to be planned, and the stressful part was not the danger itself but the fear of making a small mistake. Afterward, I read the transcript of our radio calls with the ground. In the transcript, my voice sounds calm. I did not feel calm.

Day 81. In the part of the station built by Russia, there is a small portrait of Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space. When he flew in 1961, Soviet leaders presented his flight as proof of the strength of socialism, and the space race became a contest between capitalism and socialism. Today, astronauts from Russia and the United States share this station.

Day 112. Some days bring a quiet sadness. I miss Sofia's voice and the smell of rain. We talk by video every week, but a screen cannot give a hug. When the sadness comes, I float to the window and look at the Earth. It is very blue and very thin at the edges, and from up here, there is no border on it anywhere.

Day 180. We land tomorrow. The teddy goes home in my pocket.

Questions:
Why did the writer tie a teddy bear to her seat?
When it began to float, the crew knew they had reached orbit.
Why do astronauts exercise for two hours a day?
They exercise to protect their hearts and bones, because the cardiovascular system becomes weaker without gravity.
What did the writer notice in the transcript of the radio calls?
Her voice sounded calm, although she did not feel calm.
What did Soviet leaders say Gagarin's flight proved?
They presented it as proof of the strength of socialism.
What does the writer do when sadness comes?
She floats to the window and looks at the Earth.

lessons.title: The Moon in the Courtroom
lessons.summary: How a young Abraham Lincoln used an almanac and the position of the moon to defend a man accused of killing another man.
lessons.text:
In August 1857, at a large outdoor religious meeting in Illinois, a fight broke out late at night. A man named James Metzker was badly beaten, and a few days later he died. It was a homicide, and the county had to find out who was responsible. Witnesses were ready to accuse two young men. One of them was Duff Armstrong.

The Armstrong family had known Abraham Lincoln for years, long before he became president. When Duff was a child, Lincoln had lived nearby, and Duff's mother had been kind to him when he was poor. Now she was a widow, and she asked Lincoln to defend her son. He agreed and refused to take any money.

The homicide trial took place in May 1858. The case against Armstrong depended mainly on one witness, a man named Charles Allen. Allen swore that he had seen Armstrong strike Metzker. He said that he could see clearly because the moon had been high and bright, almost as bright as day. The prosecution contended that this was enough. A witness who saw a crime by bright moonlight, they said, had no reason to lie, and no reason to accuse an innocent man.

Lincoln did not try to show that Allen was a liar. He thought that Allen might sincerely believe his own story. People who sincerely remember something can still be wrong, especially when their memory is vague and the events took place months before. So Lincoln asked Allen to repeat, again and again, exactly where the moon had been. Allen's answers became firmer each time, not more vague.

Then Lincoln produced an almanac, a yearly book that listed the times when the sun and the moon rose and set. The almanac showed that at the time of the fight, the moon had been low in the sky, close to setting. It could not have given the bright light that Allen described. The witness's credibility collapsed. If he was wrong about the moon, the jury wondered, what else was he wrong about?

Lincoln also contended that the blow might have come from someone else, and he spoke to the jury about the injustice of sending a young man to prison on the word of a witness whose credibility was now in doubt. Lincoln knew that courts make mistakes, and that an injustice done in a courtroom is very hard to undo. After a short time, the jury found Armstrong not guilty.

Later, a rumor spread that Lincoln had used a false almanac, printed for another year. Astronomers have since checked the moon's position for that night and found that the almanac was correct.

The case shows that a witness can be honest and still be wrong, and that the sky, which moves by strict rules, can be a more reliable witness than a human being.

Questions:
What happened at the religious meeting in 1857?
A fight broke out, and a man named James Metzker was badly beaten and later died.
Why did Lincoln agree to defend Duff Armstrong?
Duff's mother had been kind to Lincoln when he was poor, and she asked him for help.
What did Charles Allen say about the moon?
He said that the moon had been high and bright, almost as bright as day.
What did the almanac show?
It showed that the moon had been low in the sky, close to setting.
What happened to Allen's credibility?
It collapsed, because he was wrong about the moon.
